/-!
# Erdős Problem 333

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/333](https://www.erdosproblems.com/333)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [ErNe77] Erdős, P. and Newman, D. J., *Bases for sets of integers*. J. Number Theory (1977),
  420-425.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Asymptotics

open scoped Pointwise

namespace Erdos333

/--
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of density zero. Does there exist a $B$ such that
$A\subseteq B+B$ and
$$\lvert B\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert =o(N^{1/2})$$
for all large $N$?

The answer is no. Erdős and Newman [ErNe77] have proved this is true when $A$ is the set of
squares. In fact, Theorem 2 of [ErNe77] already implies a negative answer to this problem, but
this seems to have been overlooked by Erdős and Graham.

See also [806].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/1d7b3f00780b85ed0462e79a1cd5650ee9055655/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos333.lean"]
theorem erdos_333 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, A.HasDensity 0 →
      ∃ B : Set ℕ, A ⊆ B + B ∧
        (fun N => ((B ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop]
          fun N => Real.sqrt N := by
  sorry

end Erdos333

reformulations.difference: `A B : Set ℕ` include 0, so 0 ∈ B is allowed; it is never counted, because the Lean counts `B ∩ Set.Icc 1 N`. ErGr80 speaks of 'a set of integers', and the reading under which the problem was resolved (Woett's, on the erdosproblems forum, and the linked Lean proof) counts |B ∩ [0,N]|. Density zero is the repository's `Set.HasDensity A 0`, whose partial densities count [0,b). The site defines density with [1,N].
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (i) |B ∩ [0,N]| and |B ∩ [1,N]| differ by at most 1, and 1 = o(√N). So `(fun N => ((B ∩ Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (√·)` holds iff the same with `Icc 0 N`. I proved this ↔ in Lean for the whole right-hand side (`simp only [littleO_iff]` after the per-B lemma). (ii) The partial densities |A ∩ [0,b)|/b and |A ∩ [1,N]|/N have the same limit behaviour, so `HasDensity 0` is natural density zero. I also proved in Lean that the linked proof's density hypothesis (|A ∩ [0,N]|/N → 0) implies `A.HasDensity 0`. (iii) On 0 ∈ ℕ: if B had to consist of positive integers, the question would degenerate, since A = {1} could never be covered. The forum (Woett, citing Bloom's convention of reading 0 ∈ ℕ from context) takes the ℕ₀ reading, and the Lean follows it. Allowing 0 ∈ A is harmless: it forces 0 ∈ B at a cost of at most one element. The answer is 'no' under either reading, so `answer(False)` is correct regardless. End to end, I derived the exact statement `type_of% @Erdos333.erdos_333` from the linked proof's `main_obstruction`, using only standard axioms.

review.notes:
What I verified in Lean (scratch files in /workspace/review/):
1. `#print` shows `erdos_333 : False ↔ ∀ A : Set ℕ, A.HasDensity 0 → ∃ B : Set ℕ, A ⊆ B + B ∧ (fun N : ℕ => ((B ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun N : ℕ => √(N:ℝ))`, with `HasDensity` relative to `Set.univ` (natural density).
2. The right-hand side holds for A = ∅ (with B = ∅), so the hypothesis is satisfiable and the statement is not vacuous.
3. The linked formal proof (plby/lean-proofs, Lean v4.29.1) compiles cleanly under this checkout's Lean/Mathlib v4.33.1. A 60-line bridge then proves `type_of% @Erdos333.erdos_333` exactly from its `main_obstruction`, with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] (/workspace/review/Combined2.lean). So `answer(False)`, `research solved` and the `formal_proof` record are all correct and consistent with the source's 'DISPROVED (LEAN)'. The proof is a genuine 1400-line construction (dyadic blocks built by a greedy hitting-set argument), not a degenerate one.

What I could not read directly: ErNe77 and ErGr80 themselves. The Rényi PDF of ErNe77 is a scan and there is no OCR here, so I took the ErGr80 wording from the verbatim quote in the forum thread. The theorem docstring's remarks (Erdős–Newman for the squares; Theorem 2 already implying 'no') are copied verbatim from erdosproblems.com. Neither gap affects the verdict, because the statement's truth and meaning were checked independently.

Optional, not a defect: the file could add the solved special case the source mentions (Erdős–Newman: the squares admit such a B).
